To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(a) The nucleic acids that are sensed by the immune system are produced during infection by the replication and transcription of microbial genomes.

the molecular features of nucleic acid sensors and the chemical properties of their ligands are important determinants of their ability to distinguish self and non‐ self nucleic acids, and that viruses have exploited these properties to avoid recognition.

the molecular requirements for sensing of microbial nucleic acids are diverse and include the length, sequence and structure of the nucleic acids as well as the intracellular localization of nucleic acid sensors.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of how the host can discriminate between self and non-self nucleic acids in order to avoid immune activation by endogenous nucleic acids while ensuring the detection of microbial nucleic acids.
the molecular mechanisms of nucleic acid sensing by innate immune sensors and their implications for host‐pathogen interactions.
the molecular requirements for immune activation by microbial nucleic acids and with the mechanisms of immune evasion of viruses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the molecular characteristics of nucleic acids and their sensing by the host’s immune system remain an exciting and rapidly developing area of research.
the molecular basis of the sensing of intracellular nuclec acids is not fully understood.
the innate immune system is very good at sensing nucleic acids, but that there is still a long way to go to fully understand the underlying molecular mechanisms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the molecular features of the sensors and their ligands determine the specificity of the immune response.

the innate immune system has developed a diverse set of sensors to ensure reliable detection of microbial nucleic acids, and that the sensors are capable of recognizing the most abundant nucleic acid species of microbes, but that viruses can evade recognition by using their own nucleic acids as ligands for immune evasion.

the innate immune system has evolved sophisticated molecular mechanisms that enable it to discriminate self from non‐self nucleotides, but that viruses can exploit the limited specificity of the sensors by producing ligand mimics or nucleic acid structures that are recognized by the innate immune sensors.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the molecular characteristics of the nucleic acids that are recognized by the host sensors are highly diverse, and the sensors themselves have evolved to be able to recognize a broad range of nucleic acid structures.

nucleic acid sensors have developed specific ligand‐binding properties that allow the recognition of non‐self nucleotides, but also enable the detection of self nucleic acids, which are often modified by post‐translational modifications.
intracellular nucleic acids sensors recognize a broad variety of ligands, and the ligand specificity is determined by a combination of sequence‐specific and sequence‐independent structural features.
